question.problem: Find a point that satisfies the mean value theorem for $f(x,y)=xy$ on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ are $a=⟨0,0⟩$ and $b=⟨2,4⟩,$ respectively.
question.worked_solution:
The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that the function $f(x,y)=xy$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨0,0⟩$ and $b=⟨2,4⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,4)-f(0,0) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨2,4⟩-⟨0,0⟩) \\ 2(4)-0(0) & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,4⟩ \\ 8 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨y,x⟩, \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨{c}_{2},{c}_{1}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}8 & =∇f⟨c⟩\cdot ⟨2,4⟩ \\ 8 & =⟨{c}_{2},{c}_{1}⟩\cdot ⟨2,4⟩ \\ 8 & =2{c}_{2}+4{c}_{1} \\ 4 & ={c}_{2}+2{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{a}}{{y}_{b}-{y}_{a}} & =\frac{x-{x}_{a}}{{x}_{b}-{x}_{a}} \\ \frac{y-0}{4-0} & =\frac{x-0}{2-0} \\ \frac{y}{4} & =\frac{x}{2} \\ y & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & =2{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the equation $2{c}_{2}+4{c}_{1}=8,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}2{c}_{1}+2{c}_{1} & =4 \\ 4{c}_{1} & =4 \\ {c}_{1} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find ${c}_{2}=2{c}_{1}=2.$ So, the point $C$ that satisfies the mean value theorem is $(1,2).$
